title: AI at Work: Explore, Test, Judge
description: 75-minute Part 2 workplace AI exploration session using Google Slides as the visual backbone and ShowRunner for interaction, facilitation, and resource delivery.

steps.label: RE-ENTRY
steps.title: What stuck from Tuesday?
steps.lead: One idea, boundary, or decision you now see differently because of AI.
steps.studentTask: Submit one workplace task, decision, or responsibility you now think differently about because of Tuesday's session.
steps.roomInstruction: ONE THING YOU NOW SEE DIFFERENTLY

runbook.openWith: Tuesday we asked what AI should do. Before we add anything new, I want to know what actually stuck.
runbook.whyMatters: Retrieval makes Tuesday's learning visible and gives students ownership of the bridge into Part 2.
runbook.ask: What is one workplace task, decision, or responsibility you now think differently about because of AI?
runbook.pause: Give students 60–90 seconds to submit before reading 3–4 responses aloud.
runbook.listenFor: Consequences, human judgment, accountability, fairness, verification, task redesign, or a changed view of what should be automated.
runbook.ifQuiet: Ask: What is one task you would automate less—or more—than you would have before Tuesday?
runbook.pushFurther: What changed your mind: the capability of AI, the consequence of the decision, or who is affected?
runbook.landHere: Tuesday gave us a decision framework. Today we are going to test it against what AI is actually doing in workplaces.
runbook.transition: Let's look at the landscape before you choose where to investigate.

steps.label: USE-CASE EXPLOSION
steps.title: AI is already doing WHAT?!
steps.lead: Rapid scan: which areas would you most want to investigate?
steps.studentTask: Watch the rapid use-case tour. Then choose the TWO career areas you most want to explore.
steps.roomInstruction: DON'T MEMORIZE THE EXAMPLES · NOTICE THE PATTERN

runbook.openWith: I am going to move fast. Do not try to write everything down. Your job is to notice what work is being delegated and what humans still own.
runbook.whyMatters: Broad exposure prevents students from reducing workplace AI to ChatGPT-style writing assistance.
runbook.ask: Across these examples, is AI replacing the worker—or changing what the worker spends time doing?
runbook.pause: Move quickly through slides 3–7, then give 30 seconds for students to choose two trails.
runbook.listenFor: Drafting, summarizing, analysis, classification, recommendations, workflow execution, monitoring, and human review.
runbook.ifTheySay: AI is replacing everyone → ask which examples actually removed the human vs. changed the human's role.
runbook.ifQuiet: Ask which example surprised them most.
runbook.pushFurther: What kinds of human work become more important when execution gets cheaper?
runbook.revealWhen: Most students have chosen two areas.
runbook.landHere: AI is spreading across tasks and workflows. The transferable skill is learning how to investigate a use case rather than memorizing a tool list.
runbook.transition: Now choose one trail to investigate more deeply.

steps.label: CHOOSE YOUR TRAIL
steps.title: Where do you want to explore?
steps.lead: Pick the trail closest to your interests—not the one you think you already understand.
steps.studentTask: Choose one trail. You will use it to guide your independent exploration.

runbook.openWith: You do not all need to investigate the same thing. In fact, this works better if you do not.
runbook.whyMatters: Choice increases relevance and creates useful diversity for the later team synthesis.
runbook.ask: Which trail is closest to work you might actually care about doing?
runbook.pause: Give students a moment to commit, then form informal clusters only if it helps movement.
runbook.listenFor: Students making choices based on career curiosity rather than familiarity alone.
runbook.ifQuiet: Tell them to choose the trail they would be most curious to discuss in a job interview.
runbook.landHere: You are responsible for bringing one useful discovery back to the room.
runbook.transition: Open the resource hub. You are the researcher now.

steps.label: EXPLORE THE WILD
steps.title: You are the researcher now
steps.lead: Find something interesting enough to teach someone else.
steps.studentTask: Open the AI at Work Resource Hub. Explore 2–3 resources from your trail. Submit ONE field note: the use case, what AI does, what the human still does, one benefit, one risk, and one skill you would need.
steps.roomInstruction: EXPLORE 2–3 · CAPTURE 1 · COME BACK READY TO TEACH
steps.actionLabel: Open AI at Work Resource Hub →

runbook.openWith: This is the part where I stop being the source of information. Pick resources, investigate, and decide what is worth bringing back.
runbook.whyMatters: Students practice finding, interpreting, and judging workplace AI examples instead of receiving a curated lecture summary.
runbook.ask: What job or task is changing? What exactly is AI doing? What does the human still need to do? What could go wrong?
runbook.pause: Give the room about 15 minutes of independent exploration, then use the final 5 minutes to make sure everyone submits one strong field note.
runbook.listenFor: Specific tasks and workflows, not generic statements like 'AI helps people work faster.'
runbook.ifTheySay: This is just marketing → agree, then ask them to separate the claimed capability from the actual workflow being described.
runbook.ifQuiet: Point students to the seven field-note questions on slide 10.
runbook.pushFurther: What skill would you need to work effectively with this AI rather than simply use it?
runbook.revealWhen: You have enough field notes to see a range of careers and patterns.
runbook.landHere: The tool matters less than the relationship between task, AI capability, human judgment, and consequence.
runbook.transition: Now mix perspectives and figure out what stays the same across careers.

steps.label: TEAM PATTERN HUNT
steps.title: What stays the same across different careers?
steps.lead: Mix trails. Compare discoveries. Build the pattern from evidence.
steps.studentTask: In teams, compare your field notes. Submit ONE pattern your team sees across multiple careers: AI keeps showing up as ______ while humans keep showing up as ______.
steps.roomInstruction: AI KEEPS SHOWING UP AS… · HUMANS KEEP SHOWING UP AS…

runbook.openWith: Do not simply share articles. Your team is looking for the pattern underneath the examples.
runbook.whyMatters: Cross-case comparison turns scattered examples into transferable workplace AI literacy.
runbook.ask: What does AI keep doing across careers? What do humans keep needing to know, judge, or own?
runbook.pause: Give teams 6–7 minutes, then surface 3–4 patterns.
runbook.listenFor: AI: drafting, summarizing, researching, classifying, recommending, monitoring, executing. Humans: goals, context, quality, exceptions, relationships, decisions, accountability.
runbook.ifTheySay: Humans just check the AI → ask what exactly they are checking and whether they have authority to override it.
runbook.pushFurther: Which human responsibility becomes more valuable as AI gets more capable?
runbook.revealWhen: Teams have submitted a defensible pattern.
runbook.landHere: The repeated pattern is not 'AI does the work and humans watch.' Human value shifts toward directing, evaluating, contextualizing, and owning consequences.
runbook.transition: Now teach the room one use case worth remembering.

steps.label: USE-CASE MARKETPLACE
steps.title: Teach us one thing worth knowing
steps.lead: 90 seconds. No long presentation. Make us care.
steps.studentTask: Teams choose one use case and prepare a 60–90 second pitch: the job, what AI does, why it is useful, where humans matter, and the risk. Submit your team's one-sentence takeaway before sharing.
steps.roomInstruction: JOB → AI DOES → VALUE → HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY → RISK

runbook.openWith: You found the examples. Now you become the instructor for 90 seconds.
runbook.whyMatters: Teaching requires students to decide what matters and communicate the use case clearly enough for others to evaluate it.
runbook.ask: Would you use it, use it with safeguards, or refuse to delegate this? Why?
runbook.pause: Keep pitches fast. After each one, take one quick room reaction or challenge.
runbook.listenFor: Whether teams can name a concrete benefit and a concrete human responsibility rather than praising or rejecting AI generally.
runbook.ifQuiet: Use the slide pitch template exactly and call on the next team quickly.
runbook.pushFurther: What safeguard would make the skeptical people in the room more comfortable?
runbook.revealWhen: Several teams have shared across different trails.
runbook.landHere: Good workplace AI design is not just about capability. It is about the workflow, the guardrails, and who owns the outcome.
runbook.transition: Let's raise the stakes: what happens when AI can act, not just advise?

steps.label: HUMAN JUDGMENT CHALLENGE
steps.title: How much authority would you give an AI agent?
steps.lead: Assume the agent can research, use tools, update systems, and complete multistep work.
steps.studentTask: Choose the highest level of authority you would allow. Be ready to say what would change your answer.
steps.roomInstruction: CAPABILITY IS NOT THE SAME AS AUTHORITY

runbook.openWith: Now AI is not only generating an answer. It can take actions across systems. Where do you draw the line?
runbook.whyMatters: Agentic AI makes permissions, monitoring, approval, auditability, and human override concrete workplace design questions.
runbook.ask: What would change your answer: the consequence, the data involved, the reversibility of the action, or the quality of oversight?
runbook.pause: Vote first. Then compare people at different points on the autonomy spectrum.
runbook.listenFor: Identity, permissions, human approval, monitoring, audit trails, reversibility, consequences, and escalation.
runbook.ifTheySay: Full autonomy → ask which action they would still want logged, reversible, or escalated.
runbook.ifQuiet: Ask whether their answer changes for drafting an email vs. moving money vs. changing a patient's record.
runbook.pushFurther: Who owns the consequence when an agent takes an action that a human authorized?
runbook.revealWhen: Most students have voted and there is visible disagreement to discuss.
runbook.landHere: The future workplace skill is not merely prompting AI. It is designing the relationship between human judgment and machine execution.
runbook.transition: Bring it back to your own career.

steps.label: CAREER TRANSFER
steps.title: Build your Career AI Plan
steps.lead: Leave with one concrete next move—not a vague promise to 'learn AI.'
steps.studentTask: Submit: 1) one AI use case I should learn, 2) one human skill I need to strengthen, 3) one risk I need to understand, and 4) one workflow/tool I want to try this semester.
steps.roomInstruction: USE CASE · HUMAN SKILL · RISK · NEXT EXPERIMENT

runbook.openWith: You have seen enough examples. Now make this useful to your own future work.
runbook.whyMatters: The session should end with career transfer and a self-directed next experiment rather than passive awareness.
runbook.ask: If you were interviewing for your first professional job tomorrow, what could you say about AI that would make an employer believe you actually know how to work with it?
runbook.pause: Give students 3–4 minutes to write, then close with a few responses to the final question.
runbook.listenFor: Specific workflows, verification habits, judgment, domain knowledge, responsible use, experimentation, and evidence of learning.
runbook.ifQuiet: Prompt: 'Not I use ChatGPT. What can you demonstrate about how you investigate, test, verify, redesign work, or own outcomes?'
runbook.pushFurther: What could you build, document, or practice this semester that would prove that claim?
runbook.landHere: Your advantage is not access to AI. It is the quality of the judgment you bring to work with AI.
runbook.transition: Explore. Test. Judge. Own the outcome.
